keywords: Stick / rod / pole / twig / branch baculum, baculī n. Ancient Latin baculum, baculī n. — stick or staff, useful for a stick picked up on a walk. virga, virgae f. — slender rod, switch or twig; rāmus, rāmī m. — branch or bough. rāmulus, rāmulī m. or sūrculus, sūrculī m. — small branch, twig or shoot. Baculum cape. — Pick up the stick. Hic rāmus frāctus est. — This branch is broken. Accusative plural: rāmōs . Both vowels are long; the lemma is rāmus . pertica, perticae f. — longer pole; Morgan–Owens records the surveyor’s-rod sense. virga is the shorter/slender rod or wand; baculum the stick or staff. See also curtain rods in the household section. english: Trampoline / jumping / hopping on one foot
keywords: Trampoline / jumping / hopping on one foot petaurum, petaurī n. Ancient word Modern extension Composed phrases petaurum, petaurī n. — a trampoline in our family vocabulary. The ancient word names an acrobatic apparatus; its precise ancient construction is debated. Leo Latinus uses it for the modern trampoline. This modern sense is not a claim that Romans had modern trampolines. saliō, salīre — jump or leap. saltus, saltūs m. — a jump or leap. pēs, pedis m. — foot; the ablative is pede, with short e. In petaurō salī. — Jump on the trampoline. Altius salī. — Jump higher. Ūnō pede salī. — Jump on one foot. Ūnō agrees with masculine pede; this is an ablative of means. Ambōbus pedibus salī. — Jump with both feet. Iterum salī. — Jump again. Dēsilī. — Jump down.

english: Sailor and Waves / duvet sea game / bedtime / balance / falling / tumbling
keywords: Sailor and Waves / duvet sea game / bedtime / balance / falling / tumbling Nauta et undae Ancient words Family game Composed phrases Our bedtime sea game: Theo stands on the duvet while Dad holds a corner or side and moves it to make waves; Theo jumps, falls and tumbles. Nauta et undae means “The Sailor and the Waves.” The title is our own. Strāgulum is a broad bed-covering word, used here for the duvet without specifying its filling. strāgulum, strāgulī n. — bed covering; our practical word for the duvet in this game. angulus, angulī m. — corner. latus, lateris n. — side, with short a; distinguish lātus, “broad.” mare, maris n. — sea. unda, undae f. — wave. nauta, nautae m. — sailor. nāvis, nāvis f. — ship or boat. aequilībrium, aequilībriī n. — balance or equilibrium; applied here to keeping one’s balance. genū, genūs n.; plural genua — knee; knees. The u in the plural genua is short: no macron. moveō, movēre — move. tollō, tollere — lift. dēmittō, dēmittere — lower or let down. agitō, agitāre — move about, shake. undō, undāre — billow, undulate; intransitive in our phrases. Ancient usage includes a billowing cloak. flectō, flectere — bend. iactō, iactāre — toss about. cadō, cadere — fall. volūtō, volūtāre — roll or tumble about; use tē for “roll yourself.” stō, stāre — stand. dēsinō, dēsinere — stop or cease. Tū nauta es; hoc est mare. — You’re the sailor; this is the sea. In strāgulō stā. — Stand on the duvet. Strāgulī angulum teneō. — I’m holding a corner of the duvet. Strāgulī latus teneō. — I’m holding a side of the duvet. Strāgulum tollō et dēmittō. — I lift and lower the duvet. Strāgulum moveō ut undet. — I move the duvet so that it billows. Strāgulum undat. — The duvet is billowing. Ecce unda magna. — Here comes a big wave. Vīs undās magnās an parvās? — Do you want big waves or little waves? Undās fac. — Make waves. Genua flecte. — Bend your knees. All three vowels in genua are short in the ordinary three-syllable form. Aequilībrium servā. — Keep your balance. Undīs iactāris. — You’re being tossed by the waves. Cecidistī. — You fell. Cecidī. — I fell. Tē volūtā. — Roll around. Iterum stā. — Stand up again. Dēsine. — Stop. Iterum. — Again. The game’s imagery and example sentences are composed for Theo. Undāre describes the duvet billowing; to make it billow, we move it ( moveō, agitō ). We do not use transitive strāgulum undō , which would suggest flooding the duvet.

latin: mūnus, mūneris n.; expedītiō, expedītiōnis f.
keywords: Mission / assigned task / quest / search mūnus, mūneris n.; expedītiō, expedītiōnis f. mūnus, mūneris n. — task, duty or function; our choice for a playtime “mission.” mandātum, mandātī n. — commission, instruction or something entrusted to someone. expedītiō, expedītiōnis f. — expedition or campaign in ancient usage; our contextual application to an adventurous playtime quest. It is not presented as a verified fixed translation of a modern fantasy-game quest. investīgātiō, investīgātiōnis f. — search or investigation; use for the searching activity itself. For an adventure as a daring undertaking, the existing adventure entry prefers ausum, ausī n. . Hoc est mūnus tuum: uncum reperī. — Here’s your mission: find the hook. Eāmus thēsaurum quaesītum! — Let’s go look for treasure! The latter uses the supine of purpose after a verb of motion. These are contextual choices for conversation with Theo. The adventure and search senses need not be expressed by the same noun.
